cards.explanation: The answer is that teachers will be judged more strictly. That's the reason James gives, and he puts himself right in it. He says, “…we who teach will be judged more strictly.” (James 3:1) Notice the "we." James isn't pointing a finger from far away. He's standing in the same line as everybody else, and I respect that.

The word is "says." James writes, “If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to control his whole body.” (James 3:2) He's talking about words, friends. And since he just said we all stumble in many ways, that's a pretty high bar. I've dropped a whole tray of cookies and then said something about it I'd like to take back.

The answer is that they can guide the whole animal. James says, “When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal.” (James 3:3) Look how small that bit is next to the horse. One little piece in the mouth, and the whole animal goes where it's guided.

The answer is a very small rudder. James says ships are so large and driven by strong winds, yet “…they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined.” (James 3:4) A huge ship, a mighty wind, and a tiny rudder is what turns it. James is lining up the same lesson again: small thing, big direction.

The answer is True. James says, “In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things.” (James 3:5) Same pattern as the bit and the rudder: small part, big effect. He's putting the tongue right next to those two.

The answer is a forest. James says, “Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze.” (James 3:5) One little spark, and a whole forest is in trouble. That's what a small tongue can do with a few words, kind of like one text sent at the wrong moment.

The word is "pollutes." James says the tongue “…pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.” (James 3:6) That's a strong thing to say about something so small. James isn't joking around here, and neither am I.

The answer is False. James says animals, birds, reptiles and sea creatures are being tamed and have been tamed by man, “…but no man can tame the tongue.” (James 3:7-8) He calls it “…a restless evil, full of deadly poison.” (James 3:8) A tamed animal is one thing, but a tongue is a whole other challenge.

The answer is that we curse people made in God's likeness. James says, “With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness.” (James 3:9) Notice who's on the receiving end of the cursing: people made in God's likeness. It's the same mouth going two different directions.

The answer is False. James says, “Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this should not be!” (James 3:10) He doesn't give a ratio that makes it fine. Blessing and cursing from the same mouth just shouldn't be, and he says so loud and clear.

The answer is False. James asks, “…can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs?” (James 3:12) The answer he expects is no, since a tree doesn't grow what it isn't. And he follows it with, “Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.” (James 3:12) I'd say that settles it, friends.
